title: Persian through the ages
intro: Persian has a written history of 2,500 years. Darius the Great spoke Old Persian and had it carved in cuneiform on a cliff at Behistun; the Sasanian kings and the Zoroastrian priests wrote Middle Persian in the Pahlavi script; and from the ninth century New Persian, in Arabic letters, became the language of Rudaki, Ferdowsi – and you. In this lesson you follow 25 everyday words from Old to New Persian, see how the sounds and the grammar changed, and learn why an Iranian today can read a poem written eleven centuries ago.
goals: name the three stages of Persian – Old, Middle and New – with their scripts, dates and best-known texts
trace 25 everyday words from Old Persian through Middle Persian to today (pitar → pidar → pedar)
explain where the ezafe, the plural -ān, را and the prefix می come from
tell how the Arabic alphabet came to Persian, and read the first couplet of Rudaki's «بوی جوی مولیان»

sections.title: Three stages of Persian
sections.md:
**Old Persian** (about 550–330 BC) is the language of the Achaemenid kings. It survives almost only in royal inscriptions, written in a cuneiform script of some 36 sound signs that was probably created for the purpose under Darius. Its grammar looked like Latin or Sanskrit: three genders, several cases, endings everywhere. The great inscription at Behistun begins:

> *adam Dārayavauš xšāyaθiya vazraka xšāyaθiya xšāyaθiyānām xšāyaθiya Pārsaiy xšāyaθiya dahyūnām Vištāspahyā puça Aršāmahyā napā Haxāmanišiya*

'I am Darius, the great king, king of kings, king in Persia, king of the lands, son of Hystaspes, grandson of Arsames, an Achaemenid.' (In these transliterations *x* is *kh*, *š* is *sh*, *θ* is *th* as in *thin*.) You can already hear today's words: *xšāyaθiya* became [[شاه|shāh]], *vazraka* [[بزرگ|bozorg]], *puça* 'son' [[پسر|pesar]], and Darius himself, *Dārayavauš*, is today's [[داریوش|Dāriyush]]. A sentence later Darius says *manā pitā Vištāspa* 'my father is Hystaspes' – and *manā pitā* is, word for word, [[پدر من|pedar-e man]]: the Persian [[من|man]] 'I' comes from *manā* 'my'.

**Middle Persian** (about 300 BC to AD 900), also called **Pahlavi**, was the language of the Sasanian empire and of Zoroastrian books such as the *Bundahishn*, on the creation of the world, and the *Dēnkard*, an encyclopaedia of the faith. Its cases and genders were gone, and its grammar was already close to today's. It was written in a hard script derived from Aramaic, in which many words were spelt as Aramaic words but read in Persian: a scribe wrote the Aramaic *MLKA* 'king' and said *šāh*.

**New Persian** (from the ninth century) is the Persian you are learning. It grew out of the spoken Middle Persian of the east, took the Arabic alphabet and many Arabic words, and became a language of poetry at the Samanid court in Bukhara. Rudaki, who died in 941, is its first great poet – and his lines are still read in Iran without a dictionary.

sections.title: Twenty-five words across 2,500 years
sections.md:
Here are 25 everyday words in their three shapes. Old and Middle Persian are given in the scholars' Latin transliteration (*x* = kh, *š* = sh, *θ* = th, *ē* and *ō* are long e and o); a star (*) marks a form that is not found in the Old Persian inscriptions but is known from Avestan, the sister language of the Zoroastrian scriptures, or reconstructed.

A handful of sound changes explain most of the table:

1. **Endings fall away**: *nāman-* → *nām*, *dasta-* → *dast*.
2. **t becomes d between vowels**: *pitar-* → *pidar*, *brātar-* → *brādar*.
3. **xš becomes š (sh)**: *xšāyaθiya-* → *šāh*, *xšapa-* → *šab*.
4. **θ becomes s**: *θard-* → *sāl*, *aθanga-* → *sang*.
5. **au becomes ō, and ō becomes u in Iran**: *rauča-* → *rōz* → [[روز|ruz]], *kaufa-* → *kōf* → [[کوه|kuh]].
6. **w becomes b**: *vāta-* → *wād* → [[باد|bād]], *vazraka-* → *wuzurg* → [[بزرگ|bozorg]].
7. **Two consonants can no longer start a word**, so a vowel slips in: *brādar* → [[برادر|barādar]], *drō* → [[دروغ|dorugh]].

examples.fa: پدر و مادرم در شیراز زندگی می‌کنند.
examples.r: pedar o mādar-am dar Shirāz zendegi mi-konand.
examples.en: My father and mother live in Shiraz.
examples.note: Two words that have kept their shape for 2,500 years: Old Persian *pitar-*, *mātar-*.

examples.fa: برادرم اسب‌سواری را خیلی دوست دارد.
examples.r: barādar-am asb-savāri rā kheyli dust dārad.
examples.note: In [[برادر|barādar]] an *a* has slipped between *b* and *r*. [[اسب|asb]] comes from the Median *aspa-*; the Old Persian word was *asa-*.

examples.fa: شب‌ها از کوه باد سردی می‌آید.
examples.r: shab-hā az kuh bād-e sard-i mi-āyad.
examples.en: At night a cold wind comes down from the mountain.
examples.note: Three sound changes in one sentence: *xšapa-* → [[شب|shab]], *kaufa-* → [[کوه|kuh]], *vāta-* → [[باد|bād]].

examples.fa: دروغ در آیین ایرانیان باستان بزرگ‌ترین گناه بود.
examples.r: dorugh dar āyin-e irāniyān-e bāstān bozorg-tarin gonāh bud.
examples.en: In the religion of the ancient Iranians, the lie was the greatest sin.
examples.note: *Drauga*, 'the Lie', is the great enemy of the Behistun inscription.

examples.fa: نام این روستا در هزار سال تغییر نکرده است.
examples.r: nām-e in rustā dar hezār sāl taghyir na-karde ast.
examples.en: The name of this village has not changed in a thousand years.

examples.fa: دبیر ما ادبیات فارسی درس می‌دهد.
examples.r: dabir-e mā adabiyāt-e fārsi dars mi-dahad.
examples.note: Today a [[دبیر|dabir]] is a secondary-school teacher or a secretary; in Sasanian times a *dibīr* was a scribe, from Old Persian *dipi-* 'inscription'.

examples.fa: داریوش و کوروش هنوز نام‌های رایجی در ایران هستند.
examples.r: Dāriyush o Kurosh hanuz nām-hā-ye rāyej-i dar Irān hastand.
examples.en: Dariush and Kurosh are still common names in Iran.
examples.note: Darius is Old Persian *Dārayavauš*, Cyrus is *Kuruš*.

sections.title: Grammar then and now
sections.md:
Between Darius and Rudaki, Persian lost almost all its endings. Old Persian marked gender and case on every noun; Middle Persian had no gender and hardly any cases; New Persian inherited that simple grammar and has kept it for a thousand years. Many little pieces of today's grammar are old words worn smooth:

- The **ezafe** began as the Old Persian relative pronoun *hya* 'which, who': *kāra hya manā* 'the army which (is) mine' became Middle Persian *ī*, and today's [[سپاه من|sepāh-e man]].
- The **plural -ān** is the Old Persian genitive plural *-ānām* 'of the …s': *xšāyaθiya xšāyaθiyānām* 'king of kings' lives on as [[شاه شاهان|shāh-e shāhān]] and [[شاهنشاه|shāhanshāh]].
- **را** was the Old Persian *rādiy* 'for the sake of', Middle Persian *rāy* – which is why old texts still use it for 'for, to': [[مرا|marā]] 'for me'.
- The **prefix می** comes from Middle Persian *hamē* 'always', which gave the poets' [[همی|hami]] and then [[می|mi]].
- The verb ending **-ad** goes back to Old Persian *-atiy*: *baratiy* 'he carries', Middle Persian *barēd*, today [[می‌برد|mi-barad]].

examples.en: Persian today has no grammatical gender: «او» is used both for a man and for a woman.

sections.title: From Pahlavi to Rudaki
sections.intro: How New Persian was born – and the famous story of a poem that brought a king home. The couplet of Rudaki is quoted as it is commonly printed; note the old همی after the verb.

sentences.fa: در قرن هفتم میلادی، عرب‌ها ایران را فتح کردند و ساسانیان از میان رفتند.
sentences.r: dar gharn-e haftom-e milādi, arab-hā Irān rā fath kardand va Sāsāniyān az miyān raftand.

sentences.fa: زبان عربی زبان دین و دیوان شد، اما مردم در خانه و بازار همچنان فارسی حرف می‌زدند.
sentences.r: zabān-e arabi zabān-e din o divān shod, ammā mardom dar khāne o bāzār hamchenān fārsi harf mi-zadand.
sentences.en: Arabic became the language of religion and government, but at home and in the bazaar people went on speaking Persian.
sentences.note: [[دیوان|divān]] here means 'the government offices', not a book of poems.

sentences.fa: زرتشتیان تا چند قرن کتاب‌های خود را به خط پهلوی می‌نوشتند.
sentences.r: zartoshtiyān tā chand gharn ketāb-hā-ye khod rā be khatt-e pahlavi mi-neveshtand.
sentences.en: For several centuries the Zoroastrians went on writing their books in the Pahlavi script.

sentences.fa: اما خط پهلوی دشوار بود و بسیاری از واژه‌ها را به آرامی می‌نوشتند و به فارسی می‌خواندند.
sentences.r: ammā khatt-e pahlavi doshvār bud va besyār-i az vāzhe-hā rā be ārāmi mi-neveshtand va be fārsi mi-khāndand.
sentences.en: But the Pahlavi script was difficult: many words were written in Aramaic and read in Persian.

sentences.fa: کم‌کم ایرانیان فارسی را با الفبای عربی نوشتند، که ساده‌تر و آشناتر بود.
sentences.r: kam-kam irāniyān fārsi rā bā alefbā-ye arabi neveshtand, ke sāde-tar o āshnā-tar bud.
sentences.en: Gradually Iranians began to write Persian in the Arabic alphabet, which was simpler and more familiar.

sentences.fa: برای صداهایی که در عربی نبود، چهار حرف تازه ساختند: پ، چ، ژ و گ.
sentences.r: barā-ye sedā-hā-yi ke dar arabi nabud, chahār harf-e tāze sākhtand: pe, che, zhe o gāf.
sentences.en: For the sounds that Arabic did not have, they made four new letters: پ، چ، ژ and گ.

sentences.fa: واژه‌های عربی بسیاری وارد فارسی شد، اما دستور زبان فارسی تقریباً دست نخورده ماند.

sentences.en: Many Arabic words entered Persian, but Persian grammar remained almost untouched.

sentences.fa: نخستین شاعران بزرگ فارسی نو در خراسان و آسیای میانه پدید آمدند.
sentences.r: nakhostin shā'erān-e bozorg-e fārsi-ye now dar Khorāsān o Āsiyā-ye miyāne padid āmadand.
sentences.en: The first great poets of New Persian appeared in Khorasan and Central Asia.

sentences.fa: در آن‌جا امیران سامانی شاعران را تشویق می‌کردند که به فارسی بنویسند.
sentences.r: dar ān-jā amirān-e Sāmāni shā'erān rā tashvigh mi-kardand ke be fārsi benevisand.
sentences.en: There the Samanid princes encouraged poets to write in Persian.

sentences.fa: رودکی نابینا بود و چنگ می‌نواخت و شعرهایش را خود می‌خواند.
sentences.r: Rudaki nābinā bud va chang mi-navākht va she'r-hā-yash rā khod mi-khānd.
sentences.en: Rudaki was blind; he played the harp and sang his own poems.

sentences.fa: می‌گویند امیر نصر سامانی سال‌ها در هرات مانده بود و نمی‌خواست به بخارا برگردد.
sentences.r: mi-guyand Amir Nasr-e Sāmāni sāl-hā dar Harāt mānde bud va nemi-khāst be Bokhārā bar-gardad.
sentences.en: They say that the Samanid prince Nasr had stayed in Herat for years and did not want to return to Bukhara.

sentences.fa: یارانش از رودکی خواستند شعری بگوید تا دل امیر برای بخارا تنگ شود.
sentences.r: yārān-ash az Rudaki khāstand she'r-i beguyad tā del-e amir barā-ye Bokhārā tang shavad.
sentences.en: His companions asked Rudaki to write a poem that would make the prince homesick for Bukhara.

sentences.fa: رودکی چنگ برداشت و چنین آغاز کرد:
sentences.r: Rudaki chang bardāsht va chenin āghāz kard:
sentences.en: Rudaki took up his harp and began like this:

sentences.fa: بوی جوی مولیان آید همی / یاد یار مهربان آید همی
sentences.r: bu-ye ju-ye Muliyān āyad hami / yād-e yār-e mehrabān āyad hami
sentences.en: The scent of the Muliyan stream is coming to me; the memory of a dear friend is coming to me.
sentences.note: The Muliyan was a stream in Bukhara. [[آید همی|āyad hami]] = [[می‌آید|mi-āyad]]: in early New Persian همی could follow the verb.

sentences.fa: امیر چنان به هیجان آمد که بی‌کفش بر اسب نشست و راهی بخارا شد.
sentences.r: amir chonān be hayajān āmad ke bi-kafsh bar asb neshast va rāhi-ye Bokhārā shod.
sentences.en: The prince was so moved that he jumped on his horse without his boots and set off for Bukhara.

sentences.fa: هنوز هم بیشتر ایرانیان این بیت را می‌شناسند و بدون فرهنگ لغت می‌فهمند.
sentences.r: hanuz ham bishtar-e irāniyān in beyt rā mi-shenāsand va bedun-e farhang-e loghat mi-fahmand.
sentences.en: Most Iranians still know this couplet and understand it without a dictionary.

sections.title: Old words in living mouths
sections.md:
**Behistun.** Darius had his inscription carved high up a cliff on the road from Babylon to Ecbatana (today's Hamadan), beside a relief of himself with the defeated rebels, and then had the rock below cut away so that no one could reach it. In the 1830s and 1840s the British officer Henry Rawlinson climbed the cliff, copied the Old Persian text and used it to decipher cuneiform: Behistun did for cuneiform what the Rosetta Stone did for Egyptian hieroglyphs. The site is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

**The calendar.** Every Iranian speaks a little Avestan without knowing it. The months of the Iranian year carry the names of Zoroastrian divine beings: [[اردیبهشت|Ordibehesht]] comes from *Aša Vahišta* 'the best truth', [[خرداد|Khordād]] from *Haurvatāt* 'wholeness', [[مرداد|Mordād]] from *Amərətāt* 'immortality', [[شهریور|Shahrivar]] from *Xšaθra Vairya* 'the desired kingdom', [[بهمن|Bahman]] from *Vohu Manah* 'good mind' and [[اسفند|Esfand]] from *Spəntā Ārmaiti* 'holy devotion'.

**The Zoroastrians.** Iran's Zoroastrian communities, in Yazd, Kerman and Tehran, still pray in Avestan and keep festivals with Middle Persian names – Mehregan, Sadeh, Tirgan. In Yazd and Kerman some of them also speak their own Iranian language at home, which they call *Behdini*, 'of the good religion'.

**Names.** Our friend Dariush carries the name of Darius, *Dārayavauš*, 'he who holds firm the good'. Kurosh is Cyrus; Bahram, Ardeshir, Mitra and Anahita come from the old religion and the old kings, and Rostam, Sohrab and Tahmineh from the Shahnameh. Ask an Iranian what their name means, and you will often get a short lesson in history.

sections.title: Tips
items: Old and Middle Persian are written here in Latin letters on purpose: they were never written in the Persian alphabet, and spelling them in it would be guesswork.
Persian has changed far less in a thousand years than English. Rudaki and Ferdowsi are harder than a newspaper, but they are not a foreign language – use them for reading practice.
The w-to-b change explains many words: Middle Persian *wād* → باد 'wind', *wahār* → بهار 'spring', *wārān* → باران 'rain'.
Middle Persian *ō* and *ē* became *u* and *i* in Iran but stayed *o* and *e* in Afghanistan and Tajikistan: Iranian روز *ruz*, شیر *shir* against Dari *roz*, *sher* (lesson 6).
When a word begins bar-, dor-, ser- or kh(o)r-, think of an old double consonant: برادر < *brātar-*, دروغ < *drauga-*.
Learn the month names with their meanings – they are a small lesson in ancient Iranian religion, and Iranians are often surprised and pleased when a foreigner knows them.
